reason: Developing red blood cells need haemoglobin to carry oxygen, and the listed materials are its building blocks.
expectation: The cells will make haemoglobin as they develop.

effect: The cells have matured and contain haemoglobin; I can now assemble the plasma around them.
reaction: The developmental cutaway makes the transition to nucleus-free cells clear.
reason: Plasma consists of water with dissolved solutes, so these are a natural pair.
expectation: They will form plasma for the blood sample.

effect: The water and solutes formed plasma, ready to be combined with the blood cells.
reaction: The straw-yellow description makes the fluid component distinct.
reason: Red blood cells suspended in plasma are central to the oxygen-carrying blood sample.
expectation: The red cells will be suspended in the plasma.

effect: The attempted pairing instead added white cells and platelets to the plasma; red cells still need to be added.
reaction: The required order was not obvious, but the compatibility feedback advanced the sample.
reason: The plasma now contains the other cellular components, so adding red blood cells should complete the sample.

choice.combine: Plasma with white cells and platelets

expectation: The red cells will join the other components in the blood sample.

effect: The plasma mixture cannot currently combine with anything, so adding red cells may require another preparation first.
reaction: The assembly order is unclear after that failed attempt.
reason: Inspecting the red blood cells should reveal their available next step.
expectation: The compatibility list will show how to prepare or add the red cells.

alternatives.reason: Oxygen may need to bind haemoglobin first, but I am not sure of the required order.

effect: The inspection automatically bound oxygen to haemoglobin, leaving oxygen-bearing red cells ready to add to the plasma mixture.
reaction: The reversible binding illustration explains why haemoglobin can both pick up and release oxygen.
reason: The prepared red cells and plasma mixture are the remaining components of the blood sample.

choice.with: Plasma with white cells and platelets

expectation: The oxygen-bearing red cells will join the plasma and other blood components.

effect: The oxygen-bearing cells completed the blood sample, and the goal is complete. The final description distinguishes plasma’s transport of dissolved materials from red cells’ oxygen transport.
reaction: The final cutaway brings the separate components together clearly.

mostWorthwhile.text: Inspecting the red cells was most worthwhile: it revealed the next operation, and the resulting illustration explained reversible oxygen binding and release in low-oxygen tissues.

leastWorthwhile.text: The failed attempt to add red cells to the plasma mixture was frustrating because it did not explain why the combination was unavailable.

surprise.text: I expected red cells could be added directly to plasma, but the game required them to bind oxygen first.

arbitrary.text: That required assembly order felt arbitrary: the supplied descriptions did not explain why oxygen binding had to precede adding red cells to the sample.

continue.text: I would continue for the biological explanations and connections between structures and functions, though I would hope future combinations make their required order clearer.
